strengths: The writing is clear and easy to understand.
The authors conducted numerous experiments to verify the feasibility of the method.
This self-supervised training paradigm is quite intriguing. It combines contrastive learning with MAE-based completion to achieve better results.
The experiments conducted by the authors are highly convincing. The results in Table 4 demonstrate the benefits of decoupling views for representation learning, which can inspire future work.
The idea of using cross-reconstruction is nice.
The paper proposes a new framework to successfully bring cross-reconstruction to 3D generative field for point cloud self-supervised learning.
The writing is well-organized, clear, and easy to follow.
The experiments conducted are thorough and comprehensive.

Inspiring attempt. While other works focus on single-view reconstruction, this work attempts to recontruct one view from the other view, which is more diffucult. The experiment results show that this is a good attempt, and this work may inspire more researchers.
Thorough experiments. Multiple downstream tasks are performed, and the work acheives satisfying results.
weaknesses: In some metrics, the method performs similarly to PointM2AE, so I find the claim that it "surpasses previous single-modal self-reconstruction methods in 3D self-supervised learning by a large margin" to be overly bold.

After reading the introduction, I am still somewhat confused as to why this design works: (1) Why is Part 1 able to recover its own structural information through the structural information of Part 2? What if Part 1 and Part 2 do not overlap at all? (2) What is the approximate overlap ratio between Part 1 and Part 2? Could you provide statistical data on this?

Limited novelty: The core idea of cross-reconstruction has already been evident in numerous previous works [1][2][3], making it difficult for me to identify any particularly compelling innovation in this study.

In contrastive learning in image domain, the image augmentations typically preserve the main part of the image in different view, whereas in this setting, the cropped point clouds often represent parts of an object. This will loses some contextual information. It's unclear why this limited information is sufficient to reconstruct the local part of point cloud from another view. This aspect needs further explanation.

There is some similar self-supervised approach has been proposed in the image domain, such as [1, 2]. Though they focus on different domain, the authors should consider discussing their difference in terms of learning framework in the related work section.

The core idea of cross-view reconstruction appears to have limited novelty, as the information from view2 is likely leaked into the features of view1 during the decoding process. This makes the approach not fundamentally different from single-view reconstruction methods, despite the authors' claims. The experimental results do not convincingly demonstrate the benefits of this cross-view approach over simpler alternatives.

The view construction approach does not make sense to me. In my opinion, using one part to reconstruct another within a block is merely a specific case of block usage. The paper does not adequately explain why this approach is fundamentally different from standard block masking techniques, which also involve reconstructing one portion of the point cloud from another. The distinction between 'parts' and 'views' is not clearly defined, and the justification for treating them differently is weak. It seems that the proposed method simply applies a different form of masking, rather than introducing a novel view construction strategy.

The training framework lacks novelty. It introduces only a new relative position encoding (RPE) module and a cross-attention module in the decoder. The overall architecture is largely based on existing methods, with the main changes being the addition of these two modules. The cross-attention mechanism is a standard technique, and the RPE, while potentially useful, does not represent a significant departure from existing positional encoding methods. The paper does not demonstrate a substantial architectural innovation.

Relative position encoding is not a new concept [1, 2], and there is no specific adaptation for the 3D scenario in this work. The paper does not provide a detailed explanation of how the RPE is adapted for 3D point clouds. It is unclear whether the RPE is simply applied in a straightforward manner or if there are any modifications to account for the unique characteristics of 3D data. The lack of specific adaptation for 3D scenarios raises concerns about the novelty and effectiveness of this component.

The results are questionable. Point-DAE [3] has shown that adding augmentation is highly effective for 3D MAE tasks, achieving 88.69 on PB-T50-RS. However, in the ablation study, using only absolute position embeddings achieves just 87.7. This raises doubts about the effectiveness of the proposed 'multi-view' learning and cross-attention. What if we simply add the learned relative embedding to Point-DAE instead?
